specPoints.text: practical: investigate how extension varies with applied force for helical springs, metal wires and rubber bands

primer.text: Core practical 2 asks one question — how does extension answer to applied force? — for three test materials: a spring, a metal wire and a rubber band. This note walks both apparatus set-ups, the measurement discipline, and the analysis that turns a results table into a proportionality verdict.

lessons.title: Springs and rubber bands: the method
sourceHeadings: Experiment 1: investigating force and extension for springs and rubber bands
lessons.opening: The spring investigation hangs loads from a clamped spring and reads the stretch against a ruler. The independent variable is the applied force, the dependent variable the extension, and the pointer — the fiducial marker — is what makes the ruler readings honest.
keyPoints: The independent variable is the applied force; the dependent variable is the extension.
Each 100 g load contributes a force of 1.0 N, since 0.1 kg × 10 N/kg.
A pointer (fiducial marker) aligned with the ruler scale gives accurate length readings.
The full loading run is repeated three times on the spring so an average length can be taken at each load.
Extension is the difference between the average length under load and the original unloaded length.

low.restatement: Hang known loads, read the stretch each time, repeat three times, average, and subtract the unloaded length.
low.analogy: Weighing the same parcel on three different days before trusting the figure — repetition buys the average.
low.examPointer: Name the variables exactly: independent = force, dependent = extension.

medium.restatement: The fiducial marker exists because the ruler's scale sits behind the wire's edge: aligning a fixed pointer with the scale removes the reading angle that would otherwise bias every length.
medium.analogy: A fixed needle on a compass rim: you read the needle against the dial, never eyeball the compass centre.
medium.examPointer: Safety and accuracy marks ride together: goggles for the snap risk, G-clamp for topple risk, eye-level reading for parallax.

check.modelAnswer: To investigate how the extension of a spring, and of a rubber band, varies with the applied force.

check.stem: Name two safety precautions for the spring and rubber-band practical.
check.modelAnswer: Wear goggles in case the spring or band snaps, and secure the clamp stand with a G-clamp so it cannot topple.

check.stem: Explain why the extension, not the total length, is plotted against the applied force.
check.modelAnswer: The original length already exists at zero force; only the extra stretch answers to the load. Plotting extension isolates the stretch the force causes, so the graph reveals the material's own behaviour rather than its fixed size.

check.stem: A spring's original length is 12.0 cm; with five masses attached its average length is 15.2 cm. Calculate the extension.

lessons.title: Metal wires, analysis and accuracy
sourceHeadings: Experiment 2: investigating force and extension for metal wires
lessons.opening: The metal wire is too stiff to read directly, so a tape marker rides on the wire past a reference point. Analysis then turns the table into a graph: force against extension, a line of best fit, and a straight line whose message is proportionality.
keyPoints: The wire's extension is read from how far the tape marker moves past its reference point.
The applied force is each load's weight: mass in kg multiplied by g = 10 N/kg.
For the spring and band, extension = average length − original length; for the wire, extension = new marker reading − reference reading.
A straight line on the force-extension graph means the force is proportional to the extension.
Ruler readings are taken at eye level to avoid parallax error, and the spring is checked against its limit of proportionality.

low.restatement: Mark the wire with tape, note the reference reading, and each extension is the marker's move past that reference.
low.analogy: A thumb sliding along a ruler's edge: the thumb is the tape, the starting notch the reference.
low.examPointer: The wire's reading rule differs from the spring's — quote the right subtraction for the right material.

medium.restatement: Two error classes guard the result: parallax (read at eye level) and premature reading (wait for full extension); the proportionality verdict is only safe inside the linear region, before the limit of proportionality.
medium.analogy: Reading a speedometer from the side gives a wrong number (parallax); snapping the photo before the needle settles gives another wrong number (patience).
medium.examPointer: Graph marks: axis labels with units, even scales, line of best fit — then the verdict sentence.

check.stem: Parallax error in the ruler readings is avoided by:

options.text: Reading the ruler at eye level
options.explanation: Eye-level alignment removes the reading-angle bias of record.
Length of the ruler is irrelevant.

Guessing is the error, not the cure.

check.stem: State how the force applied by each 100 g load is calculated.
check.modelAnswer: Multiply the mass by g: 0.1 kg × 10 N/kg = 1.0 N per load.

check.stem: State the wire's extension reading rule.
check.modelAnswer: Subtract the reference-point reading from the new tape-marker reading.

check.stem: Explain why each reading is taken only after the load has fully settled.
check.modelAnswer: The spring or wire keeps stretching briefly after the load lands. Reading too early records a length that is still changing — a random error — so the of-record discipline waits for the full extension before reading.

check.stem: The tape marker reads 4.6 cm against a 1.0 cm reference point. Calculate the wire's extension.

glossary.definition: The extra stretch of a sample under load: its length under load minus its unloaded original length.
The quantity the experimenter sets: here, the applied force.
The quantity measured in response: here, the extension.
A pointer used to read the ruler scale accurately.
The point beyond which extension stops answering proportionally to force.
